analysis.one_liner: Bars Medicare drug plans and pharmacy benefit managers from steering patients to their own pharmacies.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by four senators from both parties in July 2023, never left the Senate Finance Committee and died when the Congress ended without any vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop Medicare prescription drug plans and the pharmacy benefit managers they hire from limiting which network pharmacies can fill a covered drug, a practice plans use to push prescriptions toward mail-order or specialty pharmacies they own or control. Exceptions would remain only for drugs the FDA restricts to certain facilities or that need special handling a normal pharmacy cannot provide. Plans would have to file annual reports explaining any such restrictions, and the Health and Human Services Department would report to Congress each year on how the rules were working.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, who could keep filling prescriptions at their local pharmacy instead of being pushed to a plan- or PBM-owned mail-order or specialty pharmacy. Community and independent retail pharmacies, which lose prescription volume when plans steer drugs to affiliated pharmacies, would also gain. The bill would also give network pharmacies the right to demand information about why a drug was designated "limited access," with penalties for plans that provide false or late answers [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors on Medicare and community pharmacies

how_it_helps.text: Beginning in plan year 2026, prescription drug plan sponsors and pharmacy benefit managers could not restrict or limit access to any covered Part D drug to a subset of network pharmacies, except for drugs that meet a narrow 'limited access' definition (FDA-restricted distribution, or extraordinary handling, coordination, or education needs).

Plans would have to justify any limited-access restriction in writing, keep records of the rationale, and send CMS an annual list of designated drugs, the reasons, pharmacy requirements, and how much of each drug is dispensed through retail, specialty, mail-order, or other channels — including the share dispensed through pharmacies the plan or PBM owns or is affiliated with.

Network pharmacies could request the designation rationale and requirements for a restricted drug, and a plan or PBM that gives false information or fails to respond on time would be in violation of the requirement — giving pharmacies a concrete tool against unexplained exclusions.
The Secretary of Health and Human Services would report to Congress annually, starting by the end of 2027, on compliance and on how limited-access designations affect beneficiary access.

analysis.who_pays: Prescription drug plan sponsors and pharmacy benefit managers, especially their affiliated mail-order and specialty pharmacies, which would lose the ability to consolidate dispensing volume in channels they own or favor. Plans would also bear the cost of annual reporting and written justifications, and some of that cost could show up in premiums; plans argue that steering volume to mail order lowers prices, so blocking it could raise plan costs somewhat [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug plans

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only standalone prescription drug plans (PDPs), not the Medicare Advantage plans with drug coverage that most beneficiaries are enrolled in, so the protection would reach only part of the Medicare population.

Preventing plans from steering volume to mail-order and specialty pharmacies could raise costs: plans use those channels to negotiate lower dispensing costs, and any added expense could ultimately be passed to beneficiaries through premiums — the trade-off an honest supporter has to acknowledge.

Enforcement depends heavily on paperwork: the bill's teeth are written rationales, annual reports, and a violation finding for false or late information, with no private right of action or specified penalty beyond that, so its real-world effect would rest on CMS and HHS follow-through.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to seniors — keeping the choice to use a local pharmacy rather than being routed to a plan- or PBM-owned one — is real but modest in scope, because the bill only reaches standalone Part D drug plans and relies mainly on transparency and reporting rather than penalties. The main cost falls on PBMs and their affiliated pharmacies, with a possible smaller knock-on to premiums if mail-order efficiency is lost. On balance it is a targeted consumer-protection fix, not a sweeping one, and its usefulness would have depended on regulators enforcing the reporting rules.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in July 2023, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator John Thune introduced the bill on July 20, 2023, joined from the start by Senators Sherrod Brown, John Barrasso, and Debbie Stabenow — two Republicans and two Democrats.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that referral was the last action of any kind on the bill.
The bill never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or a hearing, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and the drug plans that steer dispensing to affiliated mail-order and specialty pharmacies are better off, because no restriction was ever enacted and the status quo of limited-access designations continues unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and their affiliated pharmacies

for.name: Sen. John Thune
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate on July 20, 2023.

for.name: Sens. Sherrod Brown, John Barrasso, and Debbie Stabenow
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from both parties' leadership ranks.

for.name: Community and independent pharmacies
for.what_they_did: Would-be beneficiaries of the ban on steering prescriptions to PBM-affiliated pharmacies; the bill addresses concerns independent pharmacies have raised about being cut out of networks.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Ron Wyden)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration; after the July 2023 referral, no markup, vote, or further action ever occurred.

against.name: Pharmacy benefit manager industry
against.role: Companies managing drug benefits (including CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, and Optum Rx)
against.what_they_did: The bill's restrictions and reporting requirements targeted PBM practices; PBM trade groups have broadly opposed legislation restricting their network-steering and affiliated-pharmacy practices.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by an even 2-2 split of two Republicans (Thune, Barrasso) and two Democrats (Brown, Stabenow), and its only recorded obstacle was inaction in a committee, not a party-line vote.

industries.note: PBMs earn revenue by steering dispensing volume into mail-order and specialty pharmacies they own or control; the bill would bar that for standalone Medicare drug plans outside narrow 'limited access' exceptions and require them to justify and report any exceptions. Their gain comes directly at the cost of patients' pharmacy choice.

Independent pharmacies lose prescriptions when plans restrict a drug to a small subset of network pharmacies; the bill would keep those prescriptions available to any network pharmacy, and gives pharmacies a right to demand the plan's rationale for any restriction.

Insurers offering standalone Part D plans lose flexibility in designing pharmacy networks but gain a federal rule that applies to all competing plans equally; the main cost is annual reporting and written justifications for any limited-access designation.

These affiliated channels exist largely because plans route volume to them; the bill would force dispensing back to open pharmacy networks for most covered drugs and require public reporting of what share of restricted drugs flows through affiliated pharmacies.
